canonical_statement: The study evaluated whether conventional aggregate metrics overstate LLM discrimination in paired clinical error-detection benchmarks and introduced paired diagnostics to separate discrimination from response bias.
The evaluation covered 15 instruction-tuned LLMs across four paired clinical error-detection test sets in three languages, with four prompt-decoding configurations per model-dataset combination.
MEDEC MS-Test contained 597 notes (311 error, 286 clean) and contributed 286 matched pairs; language was English.
MedErrBench-EN contained 208 notes (104 error, 104 clean) and contributed 104 matched pairs; language was English.
MedErrBench-CN contained 200 notes (100 error, 100 clean) and contributed 100 matched pairs; language was Chinese.
MedRECT-JA contained 295 notes (190 error, 105 clean) and contributed 190 matched pairs; language was Japanese.
MedRECT-JA used 190 error notes but only 105 unique clean notes, creating many-to-one pairing that may inflate within-pair error correlation.
Evaluation was restricted to the binary error-flag task; notes were presented independently and pairing was applied post hoc to compute pairwise discrimination.
All models were evaluated zero-shot without task-specific examples or fine-tuning.
Models with 27B parameters or fewer were loaded in bf16, while the two 70B models were loaded in fp8 via vLLM because of memory constraints.
Prompting and decoding formed a 2×2 perturbation matrix: neutral versus conservative prompts crossed with greedy versus stochastic decoding.
The conservative prompt instructed models to prefer no-error when evidence was ambiguous; all prompts required Evidence, Analysis, Confidence, and Error fields.
Greedy decoding was the primary reproducible setting, supplemented by stochastic sampling to test sensitivity to sampling variability.
Traditional evaluation metrics were balanced accuracy, F1, precision, recall, specificity, MCC, and error-flag rate.
Both-Correct Rate (BCR) was defined as the fraction of matched error/clean note pairs for which the error note was flagged and the clean counterpart was cleared.

outcome.definition: Fraction of matched pairs classified correctly on both members

canonical_statement: The independence baseline for BCR was sensitivity multiplied by specificity; the independence ratio was observed BCR divided by this expected value.
BCR was shown to satisfy the deterministic bound BCR ≤ min(sensitivity, specificity), so class bias caps pairwise discrimination at the weaker marginal.
For a balanced random classifier with sensitivity and specificity of 0.5, the BCR reference level is 25%.
For prevalence-calibrated random prediction on MedRECT-JA, the BCR independence baseline was approximately 22.9%.

Evidence Contrastive Analysis (ECA) scored whether cited evidence overlapped the clinically relevant sentence on error and clean notes, using substring containment or at least 60% word coverage and character-level counting for Chinese and Japanese.
Pairs with an unparseable verdict on either member were excluded from BCR; random-assignment imputation was used as a robustness analysis.
Across all 240 runs, balanced accuracy ranged from 0.45 to 0.71.
F1 exceeded 0.5 while balanced accuracy was at or below 0.6 in 178 of 240 runs (74%).

canonical_statement: GPT-5 mini achieved 42.3% BCR on MS-Test, with F1 0.66 and balanced accuracy 0.69; its BCR remained below its 47.1% independence baseline.
Nine of 240 inference runs exceeded a 5% parse-failure rate.
Random-assignment imputation changed cross-dataset mean BCR by less than 0.5 percentage points for every model, and the same 13 of 15 models stayed below 25% BCR.
Embedding-based TP localization on 9,428 MS-Test Pred1 judgments yielded Recall@1 of 65.3% with S-PubMedBert and 67.1% with BGE-large, versus a 12.6% random baseline.
Per-model embedding Recall@1 correlated with substring TP localization at r = 0.99 for S-PubMedBert and r = 0.98 for BGE-large.
BCR rank ordering was largely stable across the four prompt-decoding configurations, although absolute values varied by as much as 36.2 percentage points.
The authors conclude that F1-based model selection can systematically favor weak pairwise discriminators in the accuracy regime observed for clinical error detection.
The authors recommend reporting paired metrics such as BCR alongside traditional metrics for safety-critical clinical NLP evaluation.
The authors position paired evaluation as a pre-adoption screening gate rather than a replacement for prospective workflow-level evaluation with clinicians.
The localization-judgment gap suggests that contrastive fine-tuning or pipelines separating localization from judgment may better target the observed failure mode.

The authors state that high-recall yes-biased models might support pre-filtering with mandatory human review, but standalone clinical error-detection deployment is not supported by the current evidence.
The study used zero-shot prompting with two prompt variants and only one inference run for each sampling-based configuration; few-shot or task-specific fine-tuning was not evaluated.
The systematic sweep covered open-weight models up to 70B and included only one proprietary reference point, GPT-5 mini on MS-Test.
Undisclosed or incompletely documented training data prevent ruling out benchmark exposure for proprietary and open-weight models.
Empirical evaluation was confined to substitution-form errors because public paired benchmarks did not release paired insertion and omission errors.

ECA substring matching was designed for single-sentence errors; MedRECT-JA multi-sentence structures reduce matching granularity, and localization can partly reflect entity salience rather than true error localization.
The analysis did not investigate internal mechanisms responsible for the localization-judgment gap.
